## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\begin{marginfigure}
\mlagentstack{0}{0}{0}{0}{100}{0}
\end{marginfigure}

_Why can an agent that is generating nothing still exhaust the memory of the machine serving it?_

Every token a model reads leaves behind computed state that later tokens attend to, and a serving system keeps that state rather than compute it again. The state occupies accelerator memory in proportion to the context an agent retains, and it occupies that memory for as long as the trajectory lives, including the seconds or minutes the agent spends waiting on a test, a search, or a person. Summed across many concurrent trajectories, this retained state can outweigh the model itself, so the number of agents a machine serves at once is set less by the model than by what the agents keep and how long they keep it. Treating the state as free produces deployments that look well provisioned and then queue, stall, or thrash under real agent traffic. Treating it as disposable throws away work that would have made the next turn cheap. The engineering problem is stewardship of a derived resource, deciding what to share among branches and turns that begin the same way, what to hold through a pause, what to move aside, and what to rebuild on demand. Those decisions live inside the serving system, yet agent builders shape them through the context they send and the waits they create, even on a hosted service they do not operate. In H·S·A terms, this is where State acquires a physical price that grows with Horizon, and that price bounds how much agent work a machine can carry.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Calculate retained attention-state memory and resident fit from model geometry, token count, and storage precision
- Calculate the memory that block allocation and prefix sharing recover from full-cap reservation and duplicated prefixes
- Distinguish compatible, available prefix reuse from the applicability of the underlying information
- Select a chunked-prefill token budget that bounds the gap between output tokens for ongoing requests
- Evaluate keep, move, and recompute policies for paused state against memory pressure and resume latency
- Analyze how residence time converts a memory-fit bound into a sustainable turn rate

:::
## Attention State as a Serving Resource {#sec-vol3-kvcache-introduction}

The connection-pool repair agent (\ref{lhs-vol3-repair-agent}) has reached a candidate revision, r18. Its targeted reproducer passes, prompting the evaluation harness to submit a fully serialized request of 32,768 tokens and launch an integration test suite that runs for 45 seconds. If the serving runtime holds the request's attention state in accelerator memory throughout that entire wait, the device sits completely idle with respect to that workflow. The model generates zero tokens during the test suite, yet its retained state pins memory that another concurrent request could put to work. Preserving that state is a deliberate systems policy, and running an agentic service requires pricing that policy against its alternatives.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/hsa_locator_s.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="H·S·A locator with the State axis highlighted."}

*State becomes a physical resource claim inside the serving system.*
:::

Earlier abstractions stop short of that physical commitment. @Sec-vol3-context-engineering established how the harness selects and refreshes prompt context for each call, and @sec-vol3-foundation-model-cost priced a cached prefix as a discounted line on the bill. Neither abstraction captures the physical footprint of the underlying computation: how many gigabytes of memory those intermediate activations consume, how many concurrent trajectories an accelerator can hold at once, or what the runtime should do with that state when an agent pauses to await tool execution. Those mechanical questions dictate whether an inference node that comfortably supports a single repair workflow can scale to sustain dozens.

Managing retained attention state is not solely an internal runtime problem; it spans an operational boundary between two parties. The application caller controls its submitted context, tool execution timing, and any cache-management hints the serving API exposes. The serving operator controls physical device allocation, memory placement, compute scheduling, and retention policies. When the two belong to separate organizations—as with hosted commercial model APIs—the caller cannot manage physical accelerator memory directly. Instead, the application influences retention only through the interfaces and pricing tiers the service exposes. Distinguishing where these responsibilities divide clarifies which performance levers belong to the agent harness and which belong to the serving runtime.

This management problem traces the physical lifecycle of attention state through the serving engine. Every active sequence retains intermediate key and value tensors across each transformer layer, and quantifying this tensor footprint against the memory pool remaining after loading model weights establishes the physical capacity envelope of an accelerator (@sec-vol3-kvcache-geometry). Naive allocators provision contiguous memory buffers sized for each request's maximum sequence length, squandering capacity through internal and external memory fragmentation (@sec-vol3-kvcache-fragmentation). Modern inference runtimes recover this stranded memory by organizing the cache into fixed-size physical blocks that support non-contiguous paging and dynamic prefix sharing (@sec-vol3-kvcache-pagedattention). Because iterative agent workflows repeatedly issue requests with shared system prompts and growing trajectory histories, runtimes index these cached blocks within tree-structured lookup hierarchies to identify and reuse matching prefixes across turns (@sec-vol3-kvcache-radix-tree).

At runtime, maintaining these state caches introduces fundamental scheduling tensions between compute-bound prompt prefill and memory-bandwidth-bound token generation, requiring runtimes to chunk prefill operations and interleave them with active decoding (@sec-vol3-kvcache-chunked-prefill). When an agent suspends execution during an external tool invocation, the serving engine must choose whether to pin that idle state in device memory, swap it to host memory or secondary storage, or evict it entirely and recompute it on demand (@sec-vol3-kvcache-swapping). Unifying these allocation, caching, scheduling, and retention mechanisms leads to an end-to-end capacity planning framework, where state residence time—rather than instantaneous memory occupancy alone—governs the aggregate throughput an inference cluster sustains (@sec-vol3-kvcache-capacity-planning).
## The Footprint of Retained Attention State {#sec-vol3-kvcache-geometry}

The r18 request's 32,768 tokens do not reach the accelerator as raw text. During causal self-attention in a Transformer decoder, each newly generated token attends to earlier tokens through their key and value projections [@vaswani2017]. Recomputing these projections at every decode step would repeat the linear transformations over the entire historical prefix, creating an unsustainable quadratic compute bottleneck. Serving runtimes avoid this recomputation by retaining the computed key and value tensors in accelerator memory across decode cycles.[^fn-kv-memory-bound] While @sec-vol3-foundation-model-autoregressive introduced this retained attention state, sustaining long-horizon agent execution requires managing its physical capacity, allocation overhead, and multi-tenant residency.

[^fn-kv-memory-bound]: **Memory-Limited Inference**: Caching keys and values trades quadratic recomputation for persistent memory capacity, and that memory quickly becomes the primary serving bottleneck. An analytical study of large-model serving revealed that sharing a single key-value head across all query heads allowed an identical deployment to serve contexts more than an order of magnitude longer, precisely because retained attention state—rather than compute throughput—bounded context length and batch concurrency [@pope2023efficiently]. Managing this memory footprint determines whether an agent deployment scales. \index{KV cache!memory bound}

::: {#dfn-kv-cache .callout-definition title="KV cache"}

***KV cache***\index{KV cache!definition} is the per-sequence store of attention keys and values that the model has computed for already processed tokens, retained so that later tokens can attend to them without recomputing their projections.

1. **Significance**: Its payload scales linearly with retained tokens; consequently, sequence context length—rather than static model parameter count—determines how many concurrent requests can share the memory pool remaining after loading model weights.
2. **Distinction**: It represents intermediate projected state rather than a raw copy or semantic compression of input text. Reconstructing it requires executing the exact token sequence through identical model weights and layer configurations.
3. **Common pitfall**: Budgeting only for input prompts. Every newly decoded output token appends key and value states at every layer, so a request reaches its maximum memory footprint at completion rather than during initial prefill.

:::

For a decoder employing causal self-attention with uniform layer geometry, every retained token contributes both a key vector and a value vector across all layers. Let $N_L$ represent the number of layers, $H_{\text{KV}}$ the number of key-value heads per layer, $d_{\text{head}}$ the dimension of each head, and $s_{\text{elem}}$ the storage size in bytes per element. Accounting for both vectors yields the memory footprint per token:

$$m_{\text{token}} = 2 \cdot N_L \cdot H_{\text{KV}} \cdot d_{\text{head}} \cdot s_{\text{elem}}$$ {#eq-mem-token}

A sequence retaining attention state across $S$ tokens requires an aggregate cache payload of $M_{\text{KV}} = S \cdot m_{\text{token}}$. Here $S$ counts only the tokens whose keys and values have already been evaluated; each newly sampled token increments $S$ once the model completes its forward pass.

The key-value head count $H_{\text{KV}}$ in @eq-mem-token represents the number of stored attention heads, which often falls below the query head count. Multi-query attention pushed this reduction to its structural extreme by sharing a single key-value head across all query heads[^fn-mqa-decode-bandwidth] [@shazeer2019fast]. **Grouped-query attention**\index{Grouped-query attention!definition} strikes an intermediate balance: several query heads share one key-value head, dividing the stored key-value head count by the group size relative to a standard multi-head design [@ainslie2023gqa]. Because this head grouping is established during pretraining, a serving allocator cannot dynamically drop heads from an existing checkpoint without fundamentally altering the model's computations.

[^fn-mqa-decode-bandwidth]: **Multi-Query Attention**: Motivated primarily by memory bandwidth rather than storage capacity—since incremental decoding reloads stored key and value tensors at each generation step—sharing key-value tensors across query heads drastically reduces memory bus traffic alongside physical storage with minimal quality loss [@shazeer2019fast]. Grouped-query attention subsequently recovered nearly all multi-head attention quality while preserving the bulk of these memory savings [@ainslie2023gqa]. Consequently, the head count $H_{\text{KV}}$ in @eq-mem-token is an architectural parameter established at pretraining. \index{Multi-query attention!memory bandwidth}

While @eq-mem-token accounts for the raw tensor payload under dense causal attention, physical memory consumption in production serving engines exceeds this theoretical bound. Allocation block granularities, memory alignment, page table metadata, and quantization scales all add runtime overhead. In addition, non-uniform architectures—such as sliding-window attention or compressed latent representations—require dedicated capacity models.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: kv-geometry-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ RETAINED ATTENTION STATE: PAYLOAD AND IDEALIZED RESIDENT FIT
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-kvcache-geometry; nbk-05-sizing-the-attention-state-for.
# │ Goal: Derive a token's KV payload and a node's unshared memory-fit bound.
# │ Show: 327,680 bytes/token; 526.0 GB pool; 195/48/12 resident sequences.
# │ How: Registry geometry and capacity, FP16 storage, local runtime reserve.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_memory, fmt_params, fmt_math

class KvGeometry:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ─────────────────────────────────
    _model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    _node = Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100
    n_layers = _model.layers
    n_kv_heads = _model.kv_heads
    d_head = _model.hidden_dim // _model.heads
    element_size = BYTES_FP16
    n_acc = _node.accelerators_per_node
    runtime_reserve = 20 * GB  # scenario: activations and runtime buffers
    ctx_short, ctx_agent, ctx_long = 8_192, 32_768, 131_072  # scenario token counts

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────
    bytes_per_token = calc_kv_cache_size(n_layers, n_kv_heads, d_head, 1, 1, element_size)
    kv_short = bytes_per_token * ctx_short
    kv_agent = bytes_per_token * ctx_agent
    kv_long = bytes_per_token * ctx_long
    node_hbm = n_acc * _node.accelerator.memory.capacity
    weights = _model.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP16)
    kv_pool = node_hbm - weights - runtime_reserve
    conc_short = int((kv_pool / kv_short).to("").magnitude)
    conc_agent = int((kv_pool / kv_agent).to("").magnitude)
    conc_long = int((kv_pool / kv_long).to("").magnitude)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────
    check(bytes_per_token.to(byte).magnitude == 327_680, "Registry KV geometry changed")
    check(525.9 < kv_pool.to(GB).magnitude < 526.1, "Expected canonical decimal-GB pool")
    check((conc_short, conc_agent, conc_long) == (195, 48, 12), "Resident-fit bounds changed")
    check(conc_agent * kv_agent <= kv_pool < (conc_agent + 1) * kv_agent, "Floor bound must bracket pool")
    check(kv_long / kv_short == ctx_long / ctx_short, "Payload must scale linearly with retained tokens")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ───────────────────────────────
    params_str = fmt_params(_model.parameters, scale="B", precision=1)
    n_acc_str = fmt_int(n_acc)
    ctx_short_str = fmt_int(ctx_short)
    ctx_agent_str = fmt_int(ctx_agent)
    ctx_long_str = fmt_int(ctx_long)
    kv_short_str = fmt_memory(kv_short, unit=GB, precision=1)
    kv_agent_str = fmt_memory(kv_agent, unit=GB, precision=1)
    kv_long_str = fmt_memory(kv_long, unit=GB, precision=1)
    node_hbm_str = fmt_memory(node_hbm, unit=GB, precision=1)
    weights_str = fmt_memory(weights, unit=GB, precision=1)
    reserve_str = fmt_memory(runtime_reserve, unit=GB, precision=0)
    kv_pool_str = fmt_memory(kv_pool, unit=GB, precision=1)
    conc_short_str = fmt_int(conc_short)
    conc_agent_str = fmt_int(conc_agent)
    conc_long_str = fmt_int(conc_long)
    token_math = fmt_math(
        rf"m_{{\text{{token}}}} = 2 \times {n_layers} \times {n_kv_heads} \times {d_head} \times {element_size.to(byte).magnitude:g} = {bytes_per_token.to(byte).magnitude:,.0f}\;\text{{bytes/token}}"
    )
    trajectory_math = fmt_math(
        rf"M_{{\text{{KV}}}} = {ctx_agent:,} \times {bytes_per_token.to(byte).magnitude:,.0f}\;\text{{bytes}} \approx {kv_agent.to(GB).magnitude:.1f}\;\text{{GB}}"
    )
    pool_math = fmt_math(
        rf"{node_hbm.to(GB).magnitude:.1f} - {weights.to(GB).magnitude:.1f} - {runtime_reserve.to(GB).magnitude:g} \approx {kv_pool.to(GB).magnitude:.1f}\;\text{{GB}}"
    )
    fit_math = fmt_math(rf"\left\lfloor {kv_pool.to(GB).magnitude:.9f} / {kv_agent.to(GB).magnitude:.9f} \right\rfloor = {conc_agent}")
```

The worked estimate uses a representative configuration: the Llama 3 70B model geometry, with `{python} KvGeometry.params_str` parameters, and a DGX H100 node containing `{python} KvGeometry.n_acc_str` accelerators. While specific hardware platforms and checkpoint dimensions vary, the underlying capacity arithmetic remains unchanged. Unlike the single-device, 8-bit illustration in @sec-vol3-foundation-model-cost, both weights and KV cache tensors use 16-bit storage here, with the model weights sharded across the node via tensor parallelism. The aggregate high-bandwidth memory remaining after provisioning model weights and a runtime reserve constitutes the **KV pool**\index{KV pool!definition}. The number of active sequences whose KV payloads can reside simultaneously within this pool defines the **resident-fit bound**\index{Resident-fit bound!definition}. This aggregate derivation assumes perfectly balanced shards without redundant weight replication; in production, memory limits must be satisfied on every individual accelerator device. @Fig-vol3-context-window-anatomy maps a 32,768-token agent context through this geometric breakdown to show how functional prompt regions translate into physical resident capacity.

::: {#fig-vol3-context-window-anatomy fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**From Agent Context to KV State**: A 32,768-token agent context (a), divided into system prompt, tool schemas, workspace, turn history, and the latest observation, becomes key and value tensors at every layer (b). The grouped-query model's per-token footprint then sets how many such contexts fit in the node's KV pool, before allocator overhead and headroom." fig-alt="Panel a divides a 32,768-token context into five labeled zones with token counts, grouped as a shared prefix, growing history, and active turn. Arrows lead to panel b, which lists model dimensions, derives 327,680 bytes per token and 10.7 GB per context, and states that resident fit equals the node's KV pool divided by the per-context footprint, so four times the context holds a quarter as many sequences."}
![](images/svg/prompt_context_window_anatomy.svg)
:::

::: {#nbk-05-sizing-the-attention-state-for .callout-notebook title="Sizing the attention state of an agent trajectory"}

**Problem**: Consider a server node provisioned with `{python} KvGeometry.node_hbm_str` of aggregate accelerator memory. Model weights occupy `{python} KvGeometry.weights_str`, and the runtime reserves `{python} KvGeometry.reserve_str` for dynamic activations and scratch buffers. Under full causal attention without prefix sharing, how many independent sequences can simultaneously reside in the remaining memory across different context lengths?

**Math**: Evaluating @eq-mem-token for this architecture yields `{python} KvGeometry.token_math`. For an agent trajectory retaining `{python} KvGeometry.ctx_agent_str` tokens, the footprint becomes `{python} KvGeometry.trajectory_math`.

Subtracting model parameters and runtime buffers isolates the usable capacity: `{python} KvGeometry.pool_math`. Dividing this available pool by the footprint per sequence and taking the floor determines the resident-fit bound. Using exact floating-point values prior to display rounding yields `{python} KvGeometry.fit_math`. @Tbl-vol3-kv-payload-fit evaluates this bound across three operational context regimes.

|         **Retained tokens**         |    **KV payload per sequence**     |        **Sequences that fit**        |
|:-----------------------------------:|:----------------------------------:|:------------------------------------:|
| `{python} KvGeometry.ctx_short_str` | `{python} KvGeometry.kv_short_str` | `{python} KvGeometry.conc_short_str` |
| `{python} KvGeometry.ctx_agent_str` | `{python} KvGeometry.kv_agent_str` | `{python} KvGeometry.conc_agent_str` |
|  `{python} KvGeometry.ctx_long_str` | `{python} KvGeometry.kv_long_str`  | `{python} KvGeometry.conc_long_str`  |

: **Payload and resident fit**: Each sequence stores its own full-attention state; the calculation excludes allocator overhead and additional headroom. {#tbl-vol3-kv-payload-fit tbl-colwidths="[28,38,34]"}

**Systems insight**: Resident capacity scales inversely with retained context length. Because model weights occupy a fixed memory slice regardless of context, expanding sequence length directly cannibalizes the cache pool. Each fourfold increase in sequence length—from `{python} KvGeometry.ctx_short_str` to `{python} KvGeometry.ctx_agent_str`, and onward to `{python} KvGeometry.ctx_long_str` tokens—reduces the resident sequence capacity by roughly 75 percent. Retained context length is the primary leverage point controlling serving capacity, and the agent runtime directly governs it. Maintaining an active working set rather than accumulating unbounded historical observations (principle \ref{pri-vol3-attention-working-set}) keeps requests operating in the high-density rows of @tbl-vol3-kv-payload-fit. Note that these figures represent raw tensor payloads; physical memory allocators, page fragmentation, and safety headroom further reduce actual capacity, while translating instantaneous resident capacity into sustainable request throughput requires analyzing sequence residence times (@sec-vol3-kv-workload-dynamics).

:::

Model weights incur a one-time memory cost that is amortized across all concurrent requests, whereas every independent sequence imposes an additive burden through its private attention state. Common prefixes across requests reduce this marginal cost only when the serving runtime systematically caches and reuses identical attention prefixes across turns.

Both model architecture and numerical precision dictate the per-token payload before memory allocation even begins. An architecture trained with fewer key-value heads or compressed latent representations[^fn-latent-kv-compression] reduces the state generated per token. Similarly, quantizing keys and values to 8-bit or 4-bit representations halves or quarters the raw element bytes $s_{\text{elem}}$, though it introduces dequantization scale metadata and potential numerical degradation that engineers must validate against target task benchmarks. Regardless of compression, every retained byte represents allocated physical memory tied to an ongoing execution lifecycle.

[^fn-latent-kv-compression]: **Latent KV Compression**: Multi-head latent attention compresses keys and values into a single low-rank latent vector per token and dynamically reconstructs per-head tensors during attention, exchanging additional projection arithmetic for a substantially smaller memory footprint [@deepseek2024v2]. Although this technique modifies the calculation of $m_{\text{token}}$ in @eq-mem-token, it preserves the fundamental system dynamics: latent cache tensors must still be paged, allocated, retained across idle periods, and evicted under memory pressure. \index{Multi-head latent attention!KV footprint}

In the running repair agent scenario, deciding whether to keep attention state resident while waiting for an external test suite to run exemplifies this lifecycle tension. Holding the attention state in accelerator memory guarantees near-instantaneous resumption when the tool returns observations, but keeping gigabytes of memory pinned for an idle agent deprives concurrent requests of accelerator resources. Before exploring eviction and caching policies, however, the serving engine must translate theoretical tensor footprints into physical memory allocations. Statically pre-allocating contiguous buffers for a sequence's maximum potential context wastes the memory pool through severe internal fragmentation long before actual tensor payloads fill device capacity.
## Memory Fragmentation {#sec-vol3-kvcache-fragmentation}

In an agentic workflow, request lengths are dynamic and fundamentally unpredictable. When an automated repair agent executes an integration test and receives a compiler traceback or test log, its next generation step requires KV cache space for both the accumulated history and the newly ingested tool output. The serving system must accommodate this growth on the fly, without knowing in advance how many tokens the model will generate or how many tool-call iterations will follow. While a static footprint calculation determines the memory consumed by tokens processed so far, the memory allocation policy governs runtime behavior: how much spare buffer to reserve at admission, whether an expanding sequence must be relocated in memory, and how rapidly reclaimed capacity returns to the shared pool.

### Reservation and growth {#sec-vol3-kv-cache-reservation-growth}

The simplest allocation strategy is **static reservation**\index{Static reservation!definition}, which provisions a contiguous memory buffer sized to the configured token cap ($s_{\max}$) the moment a request is admitted. Static reservation eliminates reallocation stalls and out-of-memory errors during generation: because the maximum possible buffer is already secured, the sequence expands within its pre-allocated envelope without moving. However, this safety incurs severe structural waste. Any unpopulated buffer capacity remains locked for the entire lifetime of the request, completely inaccessible to concurrent sequences. This reservation accounts solely for KV cache state; activation tensors and ephemeral runtime scratchpads draw from separate memory pools.

```{python}
#| label: kv-static-reservation-calc
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ STATIC RESERVATION
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-kvcache-fragmentation reservation example.
# │ Goal: Separate final-length utilization from a resident-fit bound.
# │ Show: Final-length efficiency of 6.25 percent; 48 full-cap reservations.
# │ How: Registry model and node, local cap/mean and runtime reserve assumptions.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_memory, fmt_percent
from mlsysim.physics.agents import calc_kv_cache_bytes_per_token

class StaticReservation:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
    model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    node = Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100
    elem_size = BYTES_FP16
    runtime_reserve = 20 * GB  # scenario: node-wide activations/runtime reserve
    s_max = 32_768  # illustrative deployment cap, not a model specification
    mean_final_tokens = 2_048  # hypothetical mean FINAL length, not a trace mean

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    bytes_per_token = calc_kv_cache_bytes_per_token(model, bytes_per_elem=elem_size)
    node_hbm = node.accelerators_per_node * node.accelerator.memory.capacity
    weights = model.size_in_bytes(elem_size)
    pool = node_hbm - weights - runtime_reserve
    reservation = s_max * bytes_per_token
    reservations = int((pool / reservation).to("").magnitude)
    efficiency = mean_final_tokens / s_max
    mean_doubled = 2 * mean_final_tokens  # checkpoint variation on the same scenario

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(pool.to(byte).magnitude > 0, "The KV pool must be positive")
    check(mean_doubled <= s_max, "The checkpoint variation must respect the cap")
    check(reservations * reservation <= pool < (reservations + 1) * reservation, "The count must be the whole-reservation fit bound")
    check(0 < mean_final_tokens <= s_max, "Final lengths must respect the cap")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    s_max_str = fmt_int(s_max)
    mean_final_tokens_str = fmt_int(mean_final_tokens)
    pool_gb_str = fmt_memory(pool, unit=GB, precision=1)
    reservation_gb_str = fmt_memory(reservation, unit=GB, precision=2)
    reservations_str = fmt_int(reservations)
    efficiency_str = fmt_percent(efficiency, precision=2, style="prose")
    mean_doubled_str = fmt_int(mean_doubled)
```

In the `{python} StaticReservation.pool_gb_str` KV pool modeled above, an admission cap of `{python} StaticReservation.s_max_str` tokens requires `{python} StaticReservation.reservation_gb_str` for each reservation. Dividing the pool by this single-request footprint bounds concurrency to at most `{python} StaticReservation.reservations_str` resident reservations, assuming balanced tensor-parallel sharding across accelerators and no auxiliary overhead beyond the baseline runtime reserve.

Now consider the resulting capacity utilization. If requests finish at a mean length of `{python} StaticReservation.mean_final_tokens_str` tokens, each reservation is only `{python} StaticReservation.efficiency_str` populated even upon completion—holding `{python} StaticReservation.mean_final_tokens_str` valid token states out of `{python} StaticReservation.s_max_str` allocated slots. During earlier decoding steps, utilization is lower still. Empirical evaluations confirm that this structural waste dominates naive serving systems: when @kwon2023vllm profiled early systems, actual token state accounted for only 20.4 to 38.2 percent of allocated KV memory, with the remainder lost to reservation slack and fragmentation.

A second strategy grows a contiguous allocation incrementally as tokens arrive. When adjacent capacity is unavailable in the allocator's address space, the memory manager cannot simply extend the buffer in place. Instead, it must allocate a larger buffer elsewhere, copy all existing key and value entries from the old buffer to the new buffer, and then release the original space. This approach incurs two severe penalties: the allocator must hold both buffers simultaneously during the transfer, causing transient memory spikes, and the synchronous copy consumes substantial memory bandwidth. Contiguity here refers to an unbroken span in the allocator's virtual address space. Because modern accelerators perform address translation in hardware, this contiguity restriction is not a physical hardware constraint; rather, it is imposed by standard attention kernels and legacy memory managers that require each sequence's KV tensor to occupy a single contiguous stride.

### Two kinds of unused capacity {#sec-vol3-kv-cache-unused-capacity}

Unused slots inside an active reservation constitute **internal fragmentation**\index{Internal fragmentation!definition}; free capacity split across disconnected extents too small to satisfy a contiguous request constitutes **external fragmentation**\index{External fragmentation!definition}. This classic distinction originates in early storage allocation research for multiprogrammed systems[^fn-fragmentation-internal-external] [@randell1969fragmentation]. @Tbl-vol3-kv-fragmentation-taxonomies separates them because each condition demands a distinct systems remedy: eliminating reservation slack cures the first, whereas changing the allocation granularity cures the second.

| **Condition**          | **Where capacity is unavailable**                           | **Consequence**                                                               |
|:-----------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Internal fragmentation | Inside an allocation, beyond its initialized entries        | Other requests cannot use the reserved slots                                  |
| External fragmentation | In separate free extents of a variable-size allocation pool | A contiguous request can fail even when aggregate free capacity is sufficient |

: **Unused KV capacity**: Reservation slack belongs to an allocation; external fragmentation concerns free space that cannot satisfy a particular contiguous request. {#tbl-vol3-kv-fragmentation-taxonomies tbl-colwidths="[22,40,38]"}

[^fn-fragmentation-internal-external]: **Internal and External Fragmentation**: The analysis of storage allocation that named the two losses also measured their trade: rounding requests up to fewer standard sizes cost more storage in internal fragmentation than it recovered in external fragmentation [@randell1969fragmentation]. Paged KV allocation makes the same trade on purpose, accepting at most one partial block per sequence in exchange for a pool in which any free block fits any request. \index{Fragmentation!internal versus external}

Consider a concrete example of external fragmentation. Suppose an allocator has three free extents of exactly 256 token slots each, separated by live allocations. A new sequence requiring 512 contiguous slots arrives. Even though the allocator holds 768 free slots in aggregate—more than enough capacity to satisfy the request—the allocation fails because no individual extent can accommodate 512 contiguous slots. The failure stems entirely from the contiguity requirement rather than an absolute shortage of memory.

In an agentic repair workload, this memory pressure becomes acute because a paused trajectory retains its allocation under naive retention policies while waiting for tool execution, even as concurrent requests demand memory to grow. A robust serving system therefore requires two complementary architectural mechanisms: first, a space-efficient allocation unit, which fixed-size blocks provide, and second, an explicit lifecycle and eviction policy, which @sec-vol3-kvcache-swapping develops.
## Paged KV Allocation {#sec-vol3-kvcache-pagedattention}

When an integration-test log extends an agent's repair context, the serving engine need not relocate the existing KV tensor to find a larger contiguous buffer. Instead, it allocates additional fixed-size physical blocks and appends their identifiers to the request's block table. The attention kernel dereferences that table when reading earlier token positions. PagedAttention demonstrated this combination of dynamic block allocation and noncontiguous attention over KV storage [@kwon2023vllm]. Its lineage traces directly to paged virtual memory: the Ferranti Atlas one-level store introduced paging in 1962 to decouple a program's contiguous virtual address space from scattered physical page frames [@kilburn1962onelevel]. The block table applies this same indirection to token positions, allowing sequences to grow dynamically without requiring contiguous physical allocations.

::: {#dfn-paged-kv-cache .callout-definition title="Paged KV block table"}

***Paged KV block table***\index{Paged attention!definition}\index{Paged KV block table|see{Paged attention}}\index{KV cache!block table} is a per-sequence software mapping from logical token blocks to the physical KV blocks that store their initialized key and value entries.

1. **Significance**: A sequence can grow by acquiring another block without relocating its existing blocks.
2. **Distinction**: The table maps token positions for the attention kernel; it is not the accelerator's hardware page table.
3. **Common pitfall**: A mapped block has allocated capacity, but only its initialized token entries may be read as valid KV state.

:::

### Token-to-block mapping {#sec-vol3-kv-cache-token-block-mapping}

Consider an illustrative block size of four tokens, chosen to make the mapping concrete rather than to recommend a production configuration. A ten-token prefix occupies logical blocks 0, 1, and 2. Its block table contains `[3, 7, 9]`: token positions 0–3 reside in physical block 3, positions 4–7 in block 7, and positions 8–9 in the first two slots of block 9. Physical block IDs are pool indices managed by the allocator, not raw memory addresses or token sequence numbers.

For any token position, the attention kernel determines its logical block index via integer division by the block size, consults the block table to locate the physical block, and calculates the token's offset within that block using the modulo remainder. For token position 9 with a four-token block size, the kernel calculates logical block $\lfloor 9 / 4 \rfloor = 2$, looks up physical block 9, and determines offset $9 \bmod 4 = 1$ (the second slot). Computing the final byte offset in device memory incorporates the model layer, KV head index, and tensor stride conventions. This software lookup preserves logical sequence ordering even when physical blocks are scattered across high-bandwidth memory. @Fig-vol3-pagedattention-mapping traces this ten-token lookup through the block table and previews how prefix sharing incorporates copy-on-write at block boundaries.

::: {#fig-vol3-pagedattention-mapping fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Block Table Indirection and Tail Copy-on-Write**: Panel (a) follows each logical block through its table entry to a physical block scattered among other requests' blocks; position 9 resolves to logical block 2, then to physical block 9, slot 1. Panel (b) shows two candidates that share the full blocks 3 and 7, while candidate B's private append first copies the two initialized entries of the shared tail into block 14." fig-alt="Panel a shows three logical blocks of four slots holding positions 0 to 9, arrows to a block table with entries 3, 7, and 9, and elbow arrows to physical blocks 3, 7, and 9 in a row of twelve blocks, some used by other requests. A card shows the lookup for position 9. Panel b shows candidate A's table 3, 7, 9 and candidate B's table 3, 7, 14, shared blocks 3 and 7 with two owners, and an arrow copying slots from block 9 into block 14, where position 10 is written."}
![](images/svg/paged_attention_virtual_memory.svg)
:::

Because every block in the allocator's pool is interchangeable and of identical size, any free block satisfies an allocation request. Paging thereby eliminates external memory fragmentation at block granularity. The remaining memory overhead consists of block-table metadata, temporary scratchpad buffers, and unallocated slots in each sequence's final block.

### Block size and tail waste {#sec-vol3-kv-cache-block-size-tail}

Because sequence lengths rarely align with block boundaries, the final block of a sequence typically contains uninitialized slots. This internal fragmentation constitutes the **tail waste**\index{Tail waste!definition} $\Delta_{\text{tail}}$. For a block holding $p$ tokens, tail waste is bounded by $0 \leq \Delta_{\text{tail}} \leq p-1$, with an expected value of $(p-1)/2$ when sequence lengths yield uniformly distributed remainders modulo $p$. A sequence whose length is an exact multiple of $p$ incurs zero tail waste.

Block size presents a fundamental systems trade-off:

- Smaller blocks (for example, 16 tokens) reduce worst-case tail waste and permit fine-grained prefix sharing and copy-on-write duplication. However, they inflate block-table metadata and increase indexing overhead for the attention kernel.
- Larger blocks (for example, 64 tokens) amortize bookkeeping costs and align more effectively with memory bus transactions and tensor core tile dimensions on modern accelerators, but they increase tail waste and copy overhead during branch forks.

Selecting an appropriate block size therefore requires balancing sequence length distributions, tree-search branching patterns, and hardware memory access characteristics.

```{python}
#| label: lego-05-physical-block-sizing
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PHYSICAL BLOCK SIZING
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: notebook nbk-05-sizing-physical-blocks-for-a.
# │ Goal: Convert allocation granularity into physical storage and a tail bound.
# │ Show: Node-wide block footprints and maximum tail slack for 16/64 tokens.
# │ How: Registry model geometry and precision; explicitly hypothetical sizes.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_memory, fmt_percent
from mlsysim.physics.agents import calc_kv_cache_bytes_per_token

class PhysicalBlockSizing:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
    model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    elem_size = BYTES_FP16
    small_tokens, large_tokens = 16, 64  # illustrative allocator choices
    ctx_agent = KvGeometry.ctx_agent  # scenario agent context from the footprint estimate

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    bytes_per_token = calc_kv_cache_bytes_per_token(model, bytes_per_elem=elem_size)
    small_block = small_tokens * bytes_per_token
    large_block = large_tokens * bytes_per_token
    small_tail_tokens = small_tokens - 1
    large_tail_tokens = large_tokens - 1
    small_tail = small_tail_tokens * bytes_per_token
    large_tail = large_tail_tokens * bytes_per_token
    large_tail_share = large_tail_tokens / ctx_agent  # worst-case tail share of one agent context

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(0 * byte <= small_tail < small_block, "Tail must fit inside one block")
    check(0 * byte <= large_tail < large_block, "Tail must fit inside one block")
    check(small_block * large_tokens == large_block * small_tokens, "Both block sizes must use the same KV geometry")
    check(large_tail_share < 0.005, "Prose claims the worst tail is a fraction of a percent at agent length")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    bytes_per_token_str = fmt_memory(bytes_per_token, unit=byte, precision=0)
    small_tokens_str = fmt_int(small_tokens)
    large_tokens_str = fmt_int(large_tokens)
    small_block_mb_str = fmt_memory(small_block, unit=MB, precision=2)
    large_block_mb_str = fmt_memory(large_block, unit=MB, precision=2)
    small_tail_tokens_str = fmt_int(small_tail_tokens)
    large_tail_tokens_str = fmt_int(large_tail_tokens)
    small_tail_mb_str = fmt_memory(small_tail, unit=MB, precision=2)
    large_tail_mb_str = fmt_memory(large_tail, unit=MB, precision=2)
    ctx_agent_str = fmt_int(ctx_agent)
    large_tail_share_str = fmt_percent(large_tail_share, precision=1, style="prose")
```

::: {#nbk-05-sizing-physical-blocks-for-a .callout-notebook title="Converting block size into KV storage"}

**Problem**: Given the Llama 3 70B geometry and a 16-bit KV representation, what physical storage granularity and maximum tail slack result from two candidate block sizes?

**Math**: Each token requires `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.bytes_per_token_str` across all model layers and attention heads. Multiplying that unit footprint by `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.small_tokens_str` tokens yields `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.small_block_mb_str` per block. Multiplying by `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.large_tokens_str` tokens yields `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.large_block_mb_str`. These values represent aggregate cluster-wide footprints across all model shards, not the local allocation on a single accelerator.

The maximum unused tail contains one fewer slot than a full block. A `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.small_tokens_str`-token block can therefore leave at most `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.small_tail_tokens_str` slots (`{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.small_tail_mb_str`) unutilized, while a `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.large_tokens_str`-token block can leave at most `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.large_tail_tokens_str` slots (`{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.large_tail_mb_str`) unutilized.

For a `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.ctx_agent_str`-token agent context, even the larger block's worst-case tail waste represents only `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.large_tail_share_str` of the sequence's total memory footprint.

**Systems insight**: Because tail slack is bounded by at most one block per unshared sequence, its relative overhead diminishes as sequence length increases. At multi-thousand-token agent context lengths, tail waste ceases to be the governing constraint: engineers should select block sizes primarily to optimize attention kernel throughput and sharing granularity, revisiting tail waste only when serving workloads dominated by short sequences.

:::

```{python}
#| label: kv-paged-waste-calc
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PAGED ALLOCATION PAYOFF
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-kvcache-pagedattention, paragraph after
# │          nbk-05-sizing-physical-blocks-for-a.
# │ Goal: Answer the static-reservation count with what paging admits under a
# │       stated length distribution.
# │ Show: 0.4 percent tail waste at 16-token blocks, 1.5 percent at 64;
# │       780 paged sequences vs. 48 full-cap reservations (about 16x).
# │ How: calc_expected_paged_kv_tokens over a capped-exponential length model
# │      (modeling assumption) with StaticReservation's mean, cap, and pool.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.physics.memory import calc_expected_paged_kv_tokens
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_percent, fmt_multiple

class PagedWaste:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
    block_small = PhysicalBlockSizing.small_tokens
    block_large = PhysicalBlockSizing.large_tokens
    mean_tokens = StaticReservation.mean_final_tokens  # same hypothetical mean final length
    s_max = StaticReservation.s_max
    bytes_per_token = StaticReservation.bytes_per_token
    pool = StaticReservation.pool

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    alloc_small, frag_small = calc_expected_paged_kv_tokens(mean_tokens, s_max, block_small)
    alloc_large, frag_large = calc_expected_paged_kv_tokens(mean_tokens, s_max, block_large)
    fit_paged = int((pool / (alloc_small * bytes_per_token)).to("").magnitude)
    gain = fit_paged / StaticReservation.reservations

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(0 < frag_small < frag_large < 0.02, "Larger blocks must waste more, and both only a few percent")
    check(mean_tokens <= alloc_small < mean_tokens + block_small, "Expected allocation exceeds the mean by less than one block")
    check(fit_paged == 780, "Paged fit on the canonical pool changed")
    check(15 < gain < 17, "Prose claims about sixteen times as many sequences")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    frag_small_str = fmt_percent(frag_small, precision=1, style="prose")
    frag_large_str = fmt_percent(frag_large, precision=1, style="prose")
    fit_paged_str = fmt_int(fit_paged)
    gain_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(gain))  # prose says "roughly"
```

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/kv_paged_vs_static_margin.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two horizontal bars on one linear scale: a short gray bar labeled 48 for full-cap reservation and a long green bar labeled 780 for paged blocks, with the note sequences resident, same pool."}

*Allocating blocks as tokens arrive admits about `{python} PagedWaste.gain_mult_str` the sequences of full-cap reservation.*
:::

Translating these worst-case bounds into expected memory overhead requires evaluating the workload's sequence length distribution. Consider final sequence lengths modeled as a truncated exponential distribution with a mean of `{python} StaticReservation.mean_final_tokens_str` tokens, bounded by the `{python} StaticReservation.s_max_str`-token ceiling established for static reservation. Under this distribution, `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.small_tokens_str`-token blocks leave `{python} PagedWaste.frag_small_str` of allocated KV memory unutilized, whereas `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.large_tokens_str`-token blocks leave `{python} PagedWaste.frag_large_str`.

Dividing the shared memory pool—which accommodated only `{python} StaticReservation.reservations_str` static worst-case reservations—by the expected footprint under paged allocation yields approximately `{python} PagedWaste.fit_paged_str` concurrent sequences, a `{python} PagedWaste.gain_mult_str` increase in serving capacity. This throughput multiplier represents the core payoff of paging: memory allocation expands incrementally as tokens are generated, rather than reserving buffer space for an upper bound that most requests never reach. Because this capacity figure reflects an expected value under the modeled distribution, active concurrency fluctuates dynamically with the lengths of currently executing requests.

### Copy-on-write prefix sharing {#sec-vol3-kv-cache-cow-prefix-sharing}

```{python}
#| label: kv-fork-copy-calc
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ FORK COST UNDER CONTIGUOUS ALLOCATION
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-kvcache-pagedattention, prefix-sharing paragraph.
# │ Goal: Size the tensor copy that block sharing avoids when candidates fork.
# │ Show: 10.7 GB copied for four candidates of an 8,192-token prefix.
# │ How: Registry KV geometry (PhysicalBlockSizing); scenario prefix and fan-out.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_memory

class ForkCopy:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
    prefix_tokens = 8_192  # scenario: processed prefix shared by the candidates
    branches = 4  # scenario: sampled candidate repairs
    bytes_per_token = PhysicalBlockSizing.bytes_per_token

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    copied = branches * prefix_tokens * bytes_per_token

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(branches == 4, "Prose spells out four candidates")
    check(10 < copied.to(GB).magnitude < 11, "Prose describes roughly ten gigabytes copied")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    prefix_str = fmt_int(prefix_tokens)
    copied_str = fmt_memory(copied, unit=GB, precision=1)
```

Agent workflows that sample parallel candidates to gather empirical verification (principle \ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}) make context branching frequent. Multiple candidate actions or code patches branch from an identical prompt and tool-execution prefix, diverging only in their subsequent generations. In a paged KV cache, their respective block tables point to the same physical blocks for all shared prefix tokens, provided the model architecture and runtime configuration allow block sharing.

At agent context scales, this sharing yields massive memory savings. Under contiguous allocation, deep-copying an `{python} ForkCopy.prefix_str`-token prefix across four candidate branches requires writing `{python} ForkCopy.copied_str` of KV state for the Llama 3 70B geometry. Under paged allocation, duplicating the block tables avoids copying any tensor payload whatsoever. The runtime merely updates software metadata and increments reference counters; cloning a block table requires work proportional to the number of block entries rather than the tens of gigabytes of underlying KV data.

A shared sequence tail requires special handling when branches diverge. If the final block of a shared prefix is only partially filled, two concurrent candidates cannot independently append new tokens into its remaining empty slots without overwriting each other. In the ten-token example, both candidates initially share the block table `[3, 7, 9]`. Physical block 9 contains only two valid tokens (positions 8 and 9 in slots 0 and 1). Before candidate B writes token position 10, the runtime allocates a fresh physical block 14, copies the two initialized entries from block 9 into block 14, and updates candidate B's final block-table entry to point to block 14. Candidate B then writes token 10 into slot 2 of its private block 14. This **copy-on-write**\index{Copy-on-write!KV tail}[^fn-cow-tenex-pages] operation leaves candidate A's state unchanged. @Tbl-vol3-kv-cow-trace details this ownership transition, assuming these two candidates are the sole owners of the prefix.

| **State**                     | **Candidate A table** | **Candidate B table** | **Physical ownership**                                   |
|:------------------------------|:----------------------|:----------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------|
| Before append                 | `[3, 7, 9]`           | `[3, 7, 9]`           | Blocks 3, 7, and 9 each have two owners                  |
| After B's private-tail append | `[3, 7, 9]`           | `[3, 7, 14]`          | Blocks 3 and 7 retain two owners; 9 and 14 each have one |

: **Partial-tail copy-on-write**: Full prefix blocks remain shared while the initialized portion of the tail is copied before a private append. The block IDs label allocations; they do not imply contiguous addresses. {#tbl-vol3-kv-cow-trace tbl-colwidths="[23,20,20,37]"}

[^fn-cow-tenex-pages]: **Copy-on-Write**: The TENEX time-sharing system of the early 1970s gave each page a status bit that let processes share large parts of an address space and obtain private copies of only the pages they changed [@bobrow1972tenex]. Forked candidates reuse the idea at block granularity, which is why a fan-out of sampled repairs costs private blocks in proportion to what each candidate writes, not to the prefix they share. \index{Copy-on-write!TENEX origin}

Copy-on-write is necessary only when mutating a shared, partially filled block. When a candidate branches at an exact block boundary—for instance, after a twelve-token prefix using four-token blocks—token position 12 initiates a new logical block ($\lfloor 12 / 4 \rfloor = 3$). The generating candidate simply allocates an unshared block from the free pool and appends its ID to its block table, requiring no data copying. Similarly, if a partial tail block is already privately owned (reference count of 1), the candidate appends subsequent tokens directly into the remaining slots without allocation or copying. The runtime selects the appropriate operation based on two state variables: the occupancy of the target block and its current reference count.

When an agent discards an unpromising candidate trajectory, the runtime decrements the reference counts of its constituent physical blocks. A block returns to the free pool when its reference count reaches zero and all outstanding device operations (tracked via asynchronous completion events) have finished. Furthermore, as discussed in the next section, a dormant prefix-cache entry may retain physical blocks even after an active request completes, preserving them across subsequent agent turns. Total physical memory consumption is therefore governed by the number of unique physical blocks resident on the accelerator, not the aggregate logical token count across all active candidates.

::: {#chk-05-memory-fragmentation .callout-checkpoint title="Reasoning about KV allocation"}

The allocation policy must preserve each sequence's state while managing capacity shared by many requests.

- [ ] **Reservation estimate**: If the hypothetical mean final length doubled to `{python} StaticReservation.mean_doubled_str` tokens under the same `{python} StaticReservation.s_max_str`-token cap, what fraction of each static reservation would be populated at completion, and would static reservation admit any more sequences?
- [ ] **External fragmentation**: Can you identify why the three free extents in the example cannot satisfy its contiguous request, and why a fixed-size block pool changes that condition?
- [ ] **Tail ownership**: Can you trace a private append to a shared partial tail and distinguish it from an append at a full-block boundary?
- [ ] **Reclamation**: Can you explain why ending an active request does not always make its blocks immediately reusable?

:::

Paged allocation decouples logical sequence expansion from physical memory layout, eliminating external fragmentation while enabling zero-copy prefix sharing across concurrent trajectories. However, sharing state across independent requests or across subsequent turns of an agent session requires a complementary mechanism: the serving runtime must identify matching historical prefixes across disparate requests and manage cache retention under memory pressure. That capability is the domain of prefix caching.
## Prefix Caching Across Turns {#sec-vol3-kvcache-radix-tree}

In the connection-pool repair scenario, the agent invocation that processes an integration-test result often begins with the identical system prompt, tool definitions, and historical observations present in the preceding turn. If the serving runtime retained the corresponding key-value (KV) activations from that earlier call, it can attach those existing tensors directly to the new request, prefilling only the newly arrived tokens. @Sec-vol3-foundation-model-cost priced this saving economically as prefix caching; in system implementation, it translates into a concrete serving architecture governed by an index, an explicit ownership contract, and an eviction policy.

::: {#dfn-prefix-cache .callout-definition title="Prefix cache"}

***Prefix cache***\index{Prefix cache!definition} is the serving system's index of retained KV state, keyed by exact token prefix and computation configuration, allowing subsequent requests sharing that initial sequence to attach existing state instead of recomputing it during prefill.

1. **Significance**: It converts repeated prefill work into an index lookup across request boundaries. The computational savings grow with the length of the matched prefix and recur on every turn that preserves that prefix, making stable prompt layouts essential across long trajectories.
2. **Distinction**: Block sharing reuses state among candidate sequences branched within a single forward execution; a prefix cache locates reusable state for requests arriving independently over time, retaining those activations only as long as memory pressure and eviction policies permit.
3. **Common pitfall**: Assuming a cache hit guarantees semantic freshness. Matching cached tokens verifies identical historical inputs and execution settings, but it does not check whether the real-world state described by those tokens has changed.

:::

### Prefix compatibility {#sec-vol3-kv-cache-prefix-compatibility}

In causal full-attention architectures, reusable KV state requires an exact, contiguous token prefix starting from the very first position of the sequence, rather than semantically similar phrasing. Matching token identifiers is merely the first prerequisite. The cached KV tensors remain mathematically valid only when generated under identical execution parameters: the same base model weights, active Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapters, positional encodings, and attention masks. For multimodal requests containing images, audio, or structured embeddings, matching the synthetic placeholder tokens in the text prompt is insufficient; the underlying tensor inputs and projection parameters must match exactly. A production serving engine must encode these operational dependencies directly into its cache keys or validate them before binding cached blocks to a request.

Compatibility, physical availability, and tenant isolation represent three distinct verification boundaries. Computationally compatible tensors may have already been evicted from accelerator high-bandwidth memory (HBM), or they may reside in host memory or on solid-state drives, requiring an explicit page-in transfer before the model can consume them. Conversely, tensors residing directly in local GPU memory may belong to a different tenant or security domain, making them ineligible for sharing under isolation rules. The reusable prefix length is the longest contiguous token sequence that simultaneously satisfies compatibility, physical residency, and access permissions—a sequence frequently shorter than the longest match found in the prefix tree. Furthermore, newly generated tokens qualify for subsequent prefix matching only after their corresponding KV blocks have been fully materialized in memory and committed to the index.

These structural requirements operate independently of semantic validity. Updating a target repository from commit `r17` to `r18` does not alter or invalidate the KV activations previously computed for an older prompt describing `r17`. Those tensors remain numerically identical and computationally compatible with the stale prompt, even though the context no longer reflects the current state of the code. The context-selection policies detailed in @sec-vol3-context-engineering govern which evidence to provide to the model. When the agent harness updates or replaces outdated logs in the serialized prompt, the prefix matcher detects the divergence, immediately terminates the match at the first altered token, and triggers a fresh prefill for the updated text. The prompt layout, rather than the cache layer, enforces freshness.

### Radix prefix lookup {#sec-vol3-kv-cache-radix-lookup}

A **radix prefix cache**\index{Radix prefix cache!definition} organizes stored token sequences using a compressed prefix tree (a radix tree), where each edge represents a variable-length sequence of tokens rather than a single symbol [@zheng2024sglang].[^fn-radix-patricia-trie] To resolve a cache match, the scheduler walks the tree from the root, matching prompt tokens along successive edges until reaching a divergence point. This traversal simultaneously identifies the longest common prefix and the physical KV blocks storing its activations. Once a match is identified, the runtime must acquire explicit ownership of those memory blocks before the background eviction thread can reclaim them. Lookup overhead scales with the prefix length examined, remaining on the order of microseconds on host CPUs. Alternatively, systems can implement an equivalent reuse contract using chained hash tables, where each fixed-size block is keyed by a cryptographic hash of its token content concatenated with the hash of its parent prefix.

[^fn-radix-patricia-trie]: **Compressed Prefix Tree**: The trie stored one symbol per edge, so a shared prefix was found by walking from the root [@fredkin1960]. PATRICIA collapsed chains of single-child nodes into one edge, so index size grows with the number of stored keys rather than their length [@morrison1968patricia]. The same compression matters for KV reuse, because agent prefixes run to thousands of tokens and a one-token-per-edge index would spend a node on each of them. \index{Radix tree!PATRICIA origin}

Because standard attention mechanisms allow every token to attend to all preceding positions, intermediate KV projections depend intrinsically on the full sequence history that came before them. An identical passage appearing after a modified token cannot reuse its previously computed KV activations, because altering even a single token in the prompt shifts the causal context and positional embeddings for every subsequent position. This mathematical constraint directly motivates the stable-prefix layout rules analyzed in @sec-vol3-context-engineering-staging. Staging volatile components—such as dynamic counters, tool execution outputs, or volatile scratchpad notes—toward the end of the prompt leaves the long, invariant prefix at the beginning intact. Similarly, when context compaction rewrites only trailing conversation turns, the preceding prefix remains fully reusable.

Physical memory allocation introduces a practical policy choice at block boundaries without altering the underlying definition of compatibility. Consider an agent prompt matching a ten-token prefix when using a system configured with four-token physical blocks, mapped across block identifiers `[3, 7, 9]`. The first two blocks are completely filled with eight tokens, whereas block `9` holds only two initialized entries alongside two vacant slots. A serving engine that supports partial-tail reuse can preserve all ten tokens; when a new turn appends divergent tokens, the system performs a copy-on-write operation on block `9`, copying its two valid entries into a private, mutable tail block. In contrast, an engine that caches only complete blocks reuses eight tokens and prefills the remaining two. Both designs are valid: the partial-tail strategy minimizes redundant prefill at the expense of copy-on-write buffer management, while the full-block strategy simplifies allocation by trading a modest amount of recomputation for uniform block lifecycles.

### Retention and eviction under pressure {#sec-vol3-kv-cache-retention-eviction}

When an inference request finishes, the serving engine releases the request's execution handles on the allocated KV blocks. The cache manager, however, retains its own structural references to those blocks, keeping them in memory as dormant state in case a subsequent request can reuse them. The system's retention policy determines whether the next turn finds that KV state immediately resident in accelerator memory, must page it back from host RAM, or must recompute it entirely.

Reusing and reclaiming memory blocks requires strict ownership tracking across concurrent threads and hardware streams. When a request matches a cached prefix, the memory manager increments reference counts on the corresponding blocks before dispatching execution kernels. Conversely, before reclaiming a physical block under memory pressure, the allocator must sever the cache's indexing reference, confirm that active execution references have dropped to zero, and synchronize with outstanding GPU streams that might still be reading or writing those memory addresses. Crucially, the allocator must synchronize index modifications and reference changes so that a concurrent lookup cannot bind to a block while background eviction is tearing it down.

In tree-structured prefix caches, **leaf-first eviction**\index{Leaf-first eviction!definition} maintains structural consistency by preserving contiguous paths from the root and evicting unused leaf nodes first. Because internal nodes store common prefix state shared across multiple conversation branches, evicting an ancestor would invalidate all of its downstream descendants. An internal node becomes eligible for reclamation only after all of its descendant children have been evicted. Within the set of eligible leaves, systems frequently adopt a least-recently-used (LRU) policy [@zheng2024sglang], operating on the premise that recent access predicts near-term reuse [@belady1966study].[^fn-lru-belady-optimal] @Fig-vol3-radix-tree-cache illustrates this hierarchical reclamation cascade: an inactive parent node cannot be reclaimed while its child remains cached; once the child leaf is evicted, the parent itself becomes an eligible leaf and can be freed if memory pressure persists.

::: {#fig-vol3-radix-tree-cache fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Leaf-First Eviction in a Radix Prefix Cache**: Each node stands for a run of tokens and the KV blocks that hold them, so a request's cached state is the path from the root to its node. Nodes on a running request's path stay active. Only dormant leaves are eligible, which is why the dormant Other-task node in panel (a) survives until its Final-turn child is evicted in panel (b). A least-recently-used policy would choose among the eligible leaves; it never removes an ancestor before its retained descendants." fig-alt="Two copies of a three-level tree. Panel a has an active shared-prefix root, an active repair-history node with an active test-log-turn leaf and a dormant rejected-branch leaf, and a dormant other-task node with a dormant final-turn leaf; the two dormant leaves are shaded as eligible for eviction. Panel b shows the final-turn leaf faded as evicted and the other-task node now shaded as an eligible dormant leaf. A legend defines active, dormant, eligible, and evicted."}
![](images/svg/radix_prefix_tree_architecture.svg)
:::

[^fn-lru-belady-optimal]: **Replacement with Foresight**: The classic study of page replacement showed that the optimal policy evicts the page whose next use lies furthest in the future, a rule no online system can apply because it needs the future reference string [@belady1966study]. Recency-based policies approximate it. An agent harness sometimes holds part of that future, such as a tool launch that will idle a prefix for minutes, which is why a retention hint from the caller can beat recency alone. \index{Belady optimal replacement!prefix cache}

Enforcing prefix-closed residency is an operational necessity in full-attention models. While freeing an upstream prefix block leaves the numeric values of a retained downstream suffix physically untouched, causal attention requires the entire preceding context to evaluate subsequent tokens. An orphaned suffix block is useless on the accelerator until its missing ancestral prefix is either reloaded from auxiliary storage or recomputed through a new prefill pass.

Retention policies therefore balance occupied accelerator capacity against the computational cost a future hit would eliminate. Recency alone provides an imperfect signal: an agent may generate a speculative branch that is never visited again, whereas a system prompt shared by hundreds of concurrent agent workers remains valuable despite sporadic gaps between calls. More resilient eviction schemes score cached nodes by balancing their expected reuse probability and recomputation cost against their physical memory footprint, adapting the retention weights to match dynamic workload demands.

### Prefix hit rate and the reuse contract {#sec-vol3-kv-cache-hit-rate-contract}

Counting raw matching tokens in a prompt overstates real-world system benefits whenever matching blocks have been evicted, tenant isolation policies prohibit sharing, or memory allocators round matches down to physical block boundaries. Systems engineers evaluate caching efficacy by measuring the tokens actually served from reusable KV state without recomputation. Across a specified workload window, the **token-weighted prefix hit rate**\index{Prefix hit rate!definition} is defined as

$$\rho_{\text{prefix}} = \frac{\sum_{i} S_{\text{match}}^{(i)}}{\sum_{i} S_{\text{prompt}}^{(i)}}$$ {#eq-hprefix}

where $S_{\text{prompt}}^{(i)}$ represents the prompt token count of request $i$, and $S_{\text{match}}^{(i)}$ counts the prompt tokens whose compatible KV activations were attached without recomputation after enforcing availability, security permissions, and block-alignment constraints. In the earlier four-token block example, a request matching ten tokens under a full-block-only caching policy yields $S_{\text{match}} = 8$, leaving two tokens to be prefilled. A production telemetry pipeline should also distinguish warm hits (state already resident in accelerator HBM) from cold hits (state that must be restored across PCIe from host memory).

```{python}
#| label: kv-prefix-hit-savings-calc
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ WHAT A PREFIX HIT AVOIDS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-kvcache-radix-tree, "Measuring reuse" paragraph.
# │ Goal: Put a number on the prefill work a prefix hit avoids.
# │ Show: 1.34 GB of state; ~578 + ~22 trillion operations; ~169 ms at the
# │       sustained rate; ~5 ms weight-read floor for a short suffix pass.
# │ How: Registry model/node; linear 2NS plus causal attention 2LdS^2
# │      (@eq-appdx-prefill-long); sustained rate = node peak x MfuHigh x 0.9.
# │ Note: ChunkedIteration and PausedStateChoice reuse sustained_rate.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_memory, fmt_percent, MarkdownStr

class PrefixHit:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
    model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    node = Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100
    prefix_tokens = 4_096  # scenario: invariant instructions and tool schemas
    suffix_tokens = 32  # scenario: short novel suffix appended after a hit
    utilization = Literature.Training.MfuHigh * 0.9  # scenario: sustained prefill utilization

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    n_params = model.parameters.to("count").magnitude
    bytes_per_token = PhysicalBlockSizing.bytes_per_token
    state = prefix_tokens * bytes_per_token
    linear_ops = 2 * n_params * prefix_tokens * flop
    attention_ops = 2 * model.layers * model.hidden_dim * prefix_tokens**2 * flop
    sustained_rate = node.accelerators_per_node * node.accelerator.compute.peak_flops * utilization
    t_rebuild = ((linear_ops + attention_ops) / sustained_rate).to(ms)
    weights = model.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP16)
    node_bw = node.accelerators_per_node * node.accelerator.memory.bandwidth
    t_weight_read = (weights / node_bw).to(ms)
    t_suffix_ops = (2 * n_params * suffix_tokens * flop / sustained_rate).to(ms)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(attention_ops < linear_ops, "Weight work must dominate at this prefix length")
    check(t_suffix_ops < t_weight_read, "A short suffix pass must sit below the ridge (weight-read bound)")
    check(150 < t_rebuild.magnitude < 190, "Prose describes roughly 170 ms of avoided prefill")
    check(t_weight_read < t_rebuild / 10, "The suffix floor must be far below the avoided prefill")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    prefix_str = fmt_int(prefix_tokens)
    suffix_str = fmt_int(suffix_tokens)
    state_str = fmt_memory(state, unit=GB, precision=2)
    linear_str = fmt_int(linear_ops.to(flop).magnitude / 1e12)
    attention_str = fmt_int(attention_ops.to(flop).magnitude / 1e12)
    utilization_str = fmt_percent(utilization, precision=0, style="prose")
    rate_str = fmt_int(sustained_rate.to(TFLOPs / second).magnitude)
    rebuild_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_int(t_rebuild.magnitude)} ms")
    weight_read_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_int(t_weight_read.magnitude)} ms")
```

The concrete computational value of a prefix hit follows directly from prefill arithmetic. Consider an agent workload where invariant system instructions and tool definitions form a `{python} PrefixHit.prefix_str`-token prefix. Retaining this sequence in memory occupies `{python} PrefixHit.state_str` of KV activations distributed across the server node. Reconstructing that state from scratch requires roughly `{python} PrefixHit.linear_str` trillion operations for linear projection layers, plus approximately `{python} PrefixHit.attention_str` trillion operations for causal self-attention (@eq-appdx-prefill-long). If the node sustains `{python} PrefixHit.utilization_str` of its peak 16-bit floating-point throughput—delivering about `{python} PrefixHit.rate_str` trillion operations per second—rebuilding that prefix incurs `{python} PrefixHit.rebuild_str` of prefill latency on every single cache miss. In contrast, a turn that scores a cache hit and appends only a `{python} PrefixHit.suffix_str`-token suffix bypasses the prefix prefill entirely, requiring only a single memory-bandwidth-bound pass over the model weights. Because a `{python} PrefixHit.suffix_str`-token suffix provides too little parallel arithmetic to saturate the accelerator's tensor cores, execution time is bounded by the weight-read floor of roughly `{python} PrefixHit.weight_read_str` (@eq-appdx-batched-step). Across a multi-turn trajectory, saving `{python} PrefixHit.rebuild_str` per turn compounds into a substantial reduction in both user-facing latency and aggregate server power.

Although @eq-hprefix measures the computational work avoided during prefill, end-to-end request latency also includes novel suffix prefill, autoregressive token generation, batch scheduling delays, and memory transfers—any of which can dominate total response time once a hit eliminates prefix compute. When monitoring production clusters, a declining prefix hit rate warrants investigating both sides of the client-service interface. On the client side, minor modifications in prompt serialization—such as altered whitespace, injected timestamps, or reordered JSON schema keys—prematurely truncate prefix matches. On the server side, heightened memory pressure, poor cross-node routing, or mismatched runtime configurations can render compatible state unavailable or physically inaccessible.

When utilizing hosted model APIs, application developers require an explicit reuse contract rather than relying on unverified assumptions about the provider's internal memory allocator. This contract must clearly define eligible token inputs, compatible execution configurations, tenant isolation boundaries, and supported retention lifetimes. In agentic workflows, cache expiration tightly couples this reuse contract to tool execution latency. If an external tool call blocks longer than the provider's idle eviction threshold, the subsequent turn discovers that its cached prefix has been purged and incurs a full prefill penalty—the remote equivalent of the drop-and-recompute policy described in @sec-vol3-kvcache-swapping. An agent harness aware of these eviction horizons can anticipate cache misses during long tool waits rather than absorbing unexpected latency spikes. The cached-token metric returned in API usage records is the client's primary telemetry signal, though interpreting it requires understanding its precise operational scope.

::: {#psp-05-reading-a-cached-token-count .callout-perspective title="Reading a cached-token count"}

A usage record that reports cached input tokens indicates how many prompt tokens the provider served from reusable KV state—representing the numerator of @eq-hprefix for that specific request. However, this metric remains silent on where those tensors resided (accelerator HBM vs. host DRAM), how the provider indexed them, or how long they will remain unevicted before the next invocation.

Its diagnostic value emerges when tracked across successive turns of an agent trajectory. Dividing the cached-token count by the total prompt tokens yields the caller's observed prefix hit rate. A count that abruptly plunges to zero following an extended tool execution points directly to cache expiration under idle eviction. Conversely, a count that stabilizes at a consistently lower value than expected indicates a prompt serialization divergence early in the context, halting the prefix match. Unlike server-side eviction, this layout divergence is an issue the client application can identify and resolve directly in its prompt assembly pipeline.

:::

An agent application must maintain functional correctness regardless of whether a request hits or misses the cache; the serialized context, not the cache, dictates the model's true prompt input. A cache hit simply eliminates redundant arithmetic. When an agent turn introduces a voluminous test log or extensive retrieval chunk, it inevitably injects new prefill compute into the execution engine. Scheduling that compute-intensive prefill phase alongside latency-sensitive, memory-bandwidth-bound token generation for existing requests constitutes the fundamental serving challenge addressed next.
